articles.title: Evolving role of cryoablation and cryoneurolysis for interventional pain management.
articles.abstract: Despite advances in pain management, pain remains a major global health challenge in both oncological and non-oncological patients. Long-term pharmacological treatment is often restricted by insufficient therapeutic benefit and adverse events, highlighting the need for alternative approaches such as image-guided pain therapies. The idea of treating pain with cold has been recognized for centuries, and today cryotherapy has emerged as a valuable minimally invasive option for pain management. Cryoablation refers to the destruction of tissue with extreme cold and has an increasing role, especially in the treatment of benign (e.g., osteoid osteoma), malignant bone (i.e., metastases), and soft tissue tumors, either with a curative or palliative intent. Cryoneurolysis is a related but distinct application, focusing either on peripheral nerve modulation or nerve destruction. Cryoneurolysis may be highly effective for the treatment of acute or chronic pain, including sympathetic neurolysis in cancer and non-cancer-related pain syndromes. The general approach in patients with tumor-related pain depends on whether the lesion itself can be ablated or not. In non-oncologic patients, cryoneurolysis of the responsible nerve is typically performed following a positive response to a diagnostic nerve block. Potential indications for cryotherapy are constantly evolving; however, evidence, especially for cryoneurolysis, is still limited and based mostly on single-center case series and retrospective studies. Standardized ablation protocols are lacking, and for the duration of cycles, most experts rely on imaging visualization and validated protocols. Equally important, successful integration of cryoablation and cryoneurolysis into daily practice requires structured workflows across different patient pathways and interdisciplinary management. KEY POINTS: Question Pain management remains a major global health challenge and an unmet need in oncological and non-oncological patients. Findings Cryotherapy, in terms of cryoablation and cryoneurolysis, is increasingly incorporated in multimodal curative and palliative pain care concepts, for treatment of acute and chronic pain syndromes. Clinical relevance Advancement and validation of standardized treatment protocols are needed to strengthen evidence and further enhance clinical implementation in interventional radiology practice and interdisciplinary patient care.

ISLES'24: Final stroke infarct prediction with multimodal imaging and clinical data. Where do we stand?
articles.abstract: Accurate estimation of brain infarction (i.e., irreversibly damaged tissue) is critical for guiding treatment decisions in acute ischemic stroke. Reliable infarct prediction informs key clinical interventions, including the need for patient transfer to comprehensive stroke centers, the potential benefit of additional reperfusion attempts during mechanical thrombectomy, decisions regarding secondary neuroprotective treatments, and, ultimately, prognosis of clinical outcomes. This work introduces the Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation (ISLES) 2024 challenge, which focuses on the prediction of final infarct volumes from pre-interventional acute stroke imaging and clinical data. ISLES'24 provides a comprehensive, multimodal setting where participants can leverage all clinically and practically available data - including full acute CT imaging, sub-acute follow-up MRI, and structured clinical information - across a train set of N=150 cases. On the hidden test set (N=98), the top-performing model, a multimodal nnU-Net-based architecture, achieved a Dice score of 0.285 ± 0.213 and an absolute volume difference of 21.2 ± 37.2 mL, underlining the significant challenges posed by this task and the need for further advances in multimodal learning. This overview of the ISLES'24 challenge offers two primary contributions: first, it provides a standardized, clinically realistic benchmark for post-treatment infarct prediction, built on a comprehensive, open, and multimodal longitudinal stroke imaging dataset; second, it provides insights into the strengths and limitations of current algorithms and delineates key research directions to guide the development of next-generation infarct prediction models.

articles.title: Accuracy and reliability of privacy-compliant large language models for MRI protocol selection in radiological workflows.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Accurate MRI protocolling is essential for diagnostic quality and workflow efficiency, yet manual protocol selection is time-consuming and variable. This study evaluated four contemporary open-weight large language models (LLMs) for MRI protocol and optional sequence selection from real-world clinical referrals. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, 1201 consecutive referral forms (mean age 58 ± 14 years; 646 men) were provided as unaltered text to each LLM, which selected an institutional protocol and optional sequences from predefined lists. A consensus of two board-certified radiologists served as reference. Performance was assessed at protocol and sequence levels using protocol accuracy and mean Jaccard index. RESULTS: Larger general-purpose models achieved the highest concordance with expert protocolling (GPT-OSS-120B: Jaccard 0.96, 95% CI: 0.96-0.97; accuracy 0.94, 0.93-0.95; Qwen-3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507: Jaccard 0.96, 0.95-0.97; accuracy 0.94, 0.93-0.96), outperforming MedGemma-27B-Text-IT (Jaccard 0.85, 0.84-0.87; accuracy 0.79, 0.76-0.81) and Gemma-3-27B-IT (Jaccard 0.61, 0.59-0.63; accuracy 0.58, 0.55-0.60). Unacceptable protocol selections ranged from 70/1201 cases (5.8%) for GPT-OSS and 71/1201 (5.9%) for Qwen3 to 297/1201 (24.7%) for MedGemma and 820/1,201 (68.3%) for Gemma3. Among unacceptable cases, the most common error was anatomically correct but clinically suboptimal protocol selection (57.7-70.7%), followed by incorrect anatomical region (11.6-39.4%) and optional-sequence-only errors (2.8-30.2%). GPT-OSS matched expert scan duration (p = 0.18), Qwen3 was shorter (p = 0.002), and Gemma3 and MedGemma were longer (both p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Open-weight LLMs showed high concordance with expert MRI protocolling and may support standardized protocol selection. However, clinically relevant errors persisted, underscoring the need for radiologist oversight. KEY POINTS: Question Can open-weight LLMs support accurate and standardized MRI protocol and sequence selection from clinical referrals compared with expert reference standards? Findings In 1201 referrals, LLMs achieved high concordance with expert MRI protocol selection (accuracy up to 0.94; mean Jaccard index up to 0.96), but unacceptable errors remained model-dependent and ranged from 5.8% to 68.3%. Clinical relevance Open-weight LLMs showed high agreement with expert MRI protocol decisions from clinical text and may support standardized, reliable, and scalable MRI protocolling while maintaining radiologist oversight.

articles.title: Virtual liver biopsy for detecting steatohepatitis in chemotherapy-treated patients: comparison with whole-liver radiomics and external validation.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Chemotherapy-associated steatohepatitis (CASH) increases the risk of postoperative liver failure and mortality in patients undergoing liver surgery. However, non-invasive diagnosis remains an unmet need. Radiomics has potential for characterizing liver parenchyma. This study evaluated the performance of a virtual liver biopsy for CASH prediction, comparing it with whole-liver radiomic analysis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Two retrospective series of patients undergoing hepatectomy for colorectal liver metastases were analyzed: the public "Colorectal-Liver-Metastases" dataset (training and internal validation) and a monocenter series from Humanitas Research Hospital (external validation). Inclusion criteria were preoperative chemotherapy (≥ 2 months) and post-chemotherapy CT (thickness ≤ 5 mm). IBSI-compliant radiomic features were extracted from whole-liver parenchyma and from a virtual biopsy (manually segmented 2-mL cylinder of non-tumoral liver parenchyma). Estimated liver volume (eLV) was computed using three orthogonal diameters. Four XGBoost models were developed (70/30 split, 5-fold cross-validation): clinical; clinical + VB-radiomics (ViB); clinical + VB-radiomics + eLV (ViBE+); clinical + whole-liver radiomics (WholeLiver). RESULTS: One hundred eighty patients were included: 105 internal (63 males, mean age 58.9 years, 38% CASH+) and 75 external (44 males, mean age 62.4 years, 19% CASH+). WholeLiver and ViBE+ models achieved excellent and comparable performance in internal validation (WholeLiver: AUC = 0.857 (95% BS-CI: 0.676-0.954), accuracy = 0.774 (95% BS-CI: 0.613-0.903); ViBE + : AUC = 0.831 (95% BS-CI: 0.549-0.956), accuracy = 0.839 (95% BS-CI: 0.710-0.935); p = 0.814), outperforming ViB model (AUC = 0.724 (95% BS-CI: 0.483-0.896), accuracy = 0.774 (95% BS-CI: 0.613-0.903)). SHAP analysis confirmed liver volume metrics as key predictors. In external validation, the ViBE+ model achieved AUC = 0.745 (95% BS-CI: 0.604-0.886) and accuracy = 0.680 (95% BS-CI: 0.562-0.783). CONCLUSION: Virtual biopsy provides a reproducible, non-invasive radiomic sampling strategy for CASH prediction. Combined with liver volume metrics, it achieves performance comparable to whole-liver analysis, supporting its potential clinical application. KEY POINTS: Question Despite its association with postoperative morbidity, the non-invasive preoperative assessment of CASH remains challenging in patients undergoing liver surgery. Findings Radiomic analysis based on a virtual liver biopsy, combined with volumetric measurements, showed excellent performance in predicting CASH, comparable to whole-liver analysis, with liver volume emerging as a key predictor. Critical Relevance Statement A standardized virtual biopsy-based radiomic analysis represents a promising non-invasive approach for evaluating liver parenchymal injury, as demonstrated in preoperative assessment of CASH and identification of high-risk surgical patients.

articles.title: Impact of [18F]fluoroestradiol PET/CT on clinical management in patients with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To systematically review the literature and perform a meta-analysis on the proportion of clinical management changes from [18F]fluoroestradiol ([18F]FES) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) in patients with estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Systematic review and meta-analysis conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. The study protocol was registered in the Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420261373183). MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane databases were searched until March 2026. Studies were selected using criteria based on participant, index test, and target condition framework: patients with ER-positive breast cancer, index test was [18F]FES PET/CT, and target condition was the change in management following [18F]FES PET/CT compared with conventional workup. Pooled proportions of management changes were calculated across the included studies, including subgroup and sensitivity analyses. RESULTS: Ten studies involving 773 patients were included. The pooled proportion of management changes following [18F]FES PET/CT was 38% (95% confidence interval (CI): 31-45%). Subgroup analyses showed the following: 17% (95% CI: 11-27%) for intramodality changes and 10% (95% CI: 5-21%) for intermodality changes; 17% (95% CI: 8-31%) for changes from endocrine therapy (ET) to non-ET and 12% (95% CI: 8-17%) from non-ET to ET; 6% (95% CI: 1-38%) for avoidance of additional workup and 6% (95% CI: 1-34%) prompting additional workup. Even in patients without management change, [18F]FES PET/CT was beneficial in 39% (95% CI: 24-58%) by improving diagnostic certainty and supporting current treatment options. CONCLUSION: [18F]FES PET/CT impacted management in 38% of patients with ER-positive breast cancer. KEY POINTS: Question What proportion of patients with estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer have their clinical management influenced by the results of [18F]fluoroestradiol PET/CT? Findings [18F]fluoroestradiol PET/CT impacted management in 38% of patients with ER-positive breast cancer, including inter-/intramodality changes, switches to/away from endocrine therapy, and additional diagnostic workup avoided/added. Clinical relevance [18F]fluoroestradiol PET/CT had a substantial impact on the management of patients with ER-positive breast cancer.

articles.title: Endovascular treatment of hepatic artery bleeding and pseudoaneurysms using stent-grafts: a retrospective single-centre analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate technical and clinical success rates and complications of stent-grafting for hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysms. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This single-centre retrospective study consecutively included 58 patients who underwent attempted stent-grafting for hepatic artery bleeding (n = 40) or pseudoaneurysm (n = 18) between January 2010 and June 2021. RESULTS: Technical success was achieved in 97% (56/58) of cases. Insufficient haemostasis after technical success was present in five cases (88% primary clinical success), decreasing to three cases after reintervention. In 3/5 cases, it was due to undersizing of the stent-graft, which occurred frequently, especially in vessel sizes ≥ 6 mm (n = 19, compared to the non-acute vessel diameter; n = 11, compared to the acute one). Median occlusion-free survival was 763 days. Patency rates were 81 ± 6% at 30 days and 56 ± 10% at two years. Early occlusion (≤ 30 days) was associated with significantly smaller stent-graft diameters (4.7 ± 0.7 mm vs 5.4 ± 0.7 mm; p = 0.014). In multivariate Cox regression analysis, a small diameter (4 mm) was confirmed as a risk factor for stent-graft occlusion (HR = 8.59, p = 0.006). Liver necrosis or liver failure due to insufficient collateralization occurred only in early occlusions. Median overall survival was 714 days. In 6/29 documented deaths, mortality was procedure-related (four because of insufficient haemostasis, with two after technical failure and two after technical success, and two because of fatal liver failure after stent-graft occlusion). CONCLUSION: Stent-grafting is effective for managing hepatic artery bleeding, but precise sizing is crucial, as undersizing and small diameters increase the risk of inadequate haemostasis and occlusion. KEY POINTS: Question What are the technical and clinical outcomes of stent-graft treatment for hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm, and which factors influence these outcomes? Findings Stent-graft treatment achieved high technical and clinical success rates. Stent-graft undersizing and smaller stent-graft diameters were associated with inadequate haemostasis and occlusion. Clinical relevance Stent-graft treatment is an effective option for managing hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm in critically ill patients. Accurate stent-graft sizing is a key determinant of clinical success.

articles.title: TotalSpineSeg: automated whole-spine vertebral segmentation with high robustness to labeling errors.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop TotalSpineSeg, a robust tool for vertebrae and intervertebral disc instance segmentation, along with spinal cord and spinal canal segmentation, capable of processing any 3D medical image regardless of contrast, resolution, or field of view, while overcoming fusion and fragmentation errors common in standard segmentation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A two-stage cascaded deep learning model was trained on 1404 MRIs. To explicitly prevent errors where adjacent vertebrae merge or a single vertebra splits, the architecture employs a novel "odd/even" representation. The second stage is conditioned on an odd-intervertebral disc mask from the first stage to assign distinct semantic classes to alternating vertebrae, enforcing accurate separation between neighboring vertebrae. Finally, a landmark-based logic uses key anatomical points (C2-C3, C7-T1, T12-L1, and L5-S) to anchor sequential labeling, while a localizer-based strategy ensures accurate identification even in truncated, short field-of-view scans. RESULTS: Evaluation across diverse contrasts and pathologies yielded a vertebral identification rate of 96.22% on localizer MRI and generalized to CT scans with a 92.87% identification rate. For intervertebral disc instance labeling, where vertebral separation is not mandatory, both model stages attained 99% labeling accuracy with a mean positional L2 error of 1.55 mm, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. CONCLUSION: TotalSpineSeg successfully generalizes to diverse 3D medical images, overcoming variations in contrast, resolution, and field of view. The proposed topological constraints effectively eliminate vertebral fusion and fragmentation errors, delivering a state-of-the-art identification rate for both vertebrae and intervertebral discs across MRI and CT modalities. KEY POINTS: Question Can a topology-constrained framework overcome heterogeneous contrasts and resolution limits, including localizers, to ensure robust, automated vertebral and disc labeling? Findings TotalSpineSeg achieved a high identification rate across diverse contrasts, localizers, and CT, surpassing state-of-the-art methods by eliminating fusion and fragmentation errors. Clinical relevance TotalSpineSeg enables fully automated biomarker extraction from clinical scans, allowing precise assessment of stenosis, lesions, and atrophy against normative ranges.

articles.title: Photon-counting detector CT for gastric cancer T staging: a comparative assessment with conventional energy integrating detector CT.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) for gastric cancer T staging compared with conventional energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Fifty-three patients with preoperative PCD-CT and 54 patients with preoperative EID-CT were retrospectively enrolled. Two radiologists independently assessed the visibility and T stages using all available sequences, including virtual monoenergetic images (VMIs) from PCD-CT at 40, 50, 60, and 70 kiloelectron volt (keV) levels. The lesion detectability and diagnostic accuracy of the two CT systems were analyzed and compared. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of gastric cancer lesions were also measured. RESULTS: Five lesions in the PCD-CT group and 12 lesions in the EID-CT group could not be confidently identified. For visible lesions, the overall T staging accuracies were 85.4% (95% CI: 72.8-92.8%) for Reader 1 and 83.3% (95% CI: 70.4-91.3%) for Reader 2 on PCD-CT, compared with 73.8% (95% CI: 58.9-84.7%) for Reader 1 and 78.6% (95% CI: 64.1-88.3%) for Reader 2 on EID-CT. The interobserver agreement for both CT systems was excellent, with weighted kappa values of 0.807 (95% CI: 0.693-0.921) for PCD-CT and 0.832 (95% CI: 0.720-0.943) for EID-CT. Quantitative analysis showed significantly higher SNR and CNR on PCD-CT than EID-CT (both p < 0.05). CONCLUSION: PCD-CT demonstrated significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory retrospective comparison. The potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging warrants further validation. KEY POINTS: Question The diagnostic performance and potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging are still unclear. Findings PCD-CT showed significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory comparison. Clinical relevance PCD-CT may offer potential value in gastric cancer T staging.

articles.title: Systolic pressure gradient across myocardial bridge mediates the effect of bridge depth on clinical symptoms.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The relationship between myocardial bridging (MB) morphology and function and the pathways to clinical symptoms remained unclear. This study investigated the association between delta coronary computed tomographic angiography-derived fractional flow reserve (ΔCT-FFR) and angina-equivalent symptoms in left anterior descending MB without coronary atherosclerosis using photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT). MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort included 180 patients with deep MB (depth > 2 mm) and no plaques. All underwent PCD-CT angiography. CT-FFR was computed by machine learning; systolic (ΔCT-FFRsys) and diastolic (ΔCT-FFRdia) trans-bridge pressure gradients were derived. MB depth and length were measured. Associations with symptoms were assessed by logistic regression and mediation analysis. RESULTS: Symptomatic patients (n = 81) had greater depth (median 3.30 mm vs. 2.45 mm), longer length (mean 36.06 mm vs. 26.10 mm), higher ΔCT-FFRsys (3.81% vs. 1.62%) and ΔCT-FFRdia (3.45% vs. 2.15%) than asymptomatic patients (n = 99) (all p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis identified depth (OR = 1.77, 95% CI: 1.27-2.46, p = 0.001) and ΔCT-FFRsys (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.05-1.27, p = 0.002) as independent predictors. Mediation analysis indicated that ΔCT-FFRsys significantly mediated the effect of depth on symptoms (indirect effect = 0.1881, 95% CI: 0.1023-0.2897). CONCLUSIONS: MB depth and ΔCT-FFRsys were independent risk factors for symptoms, and ΔCT-FFRsys appeared to mediate the morphological-clinical symptoms link. These findings suggested that integrated assessment, particularly ΔCT-FFRsys, might be a new non-invasive imaging biomarker for clinically identify symptomatic MB and understand its potential pathogenic mechanisms. KEY POINTS: Question The precise relationship between myocardial bridging morphological and functional features and clinical symptoms, and whether underlying key mediating factors exist, remains currently incompletely determined. Findings Depth, length, and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient of myocardial bridging independently predicted symptoms, with the gradient significantly mediating the relationship between morphology and clinical presentation. Clinical relevance Noninvasive assessment of depth and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient can assist in identifying patients with symptomatic myocardial bridging, serving as potential imaging biomarkers and providing insights into the underlying pathophysiology of symptom presentation.

articles.title: ESOI-ESUR multicentre validation of a structured MRI report for cervical cancer staging.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare an International Federation of Gyneology and Obstetrics (FIGO)-anchored structured MRI report with conventional narrative reporting for cervical cancer staging by evaluating referring clinicians' satisfaction. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this prospective multicentre crossover study (January-June 2024), consecutive patients with biopsy-proven cervical cancer at any FIGO stage underwent staging MRI at five European centres. For each patient, one narrative and one structured report were produced and independently evaluated by gynaecologists and radiation oncologists using a 12-item questionnaire (5-point Likert scale): five general items (Q1-Q5) for both formats and seven feature-specific items (Q6-Q12) for structured reports only. The primary endpoint was the proportion of structured-report evaluations with an overall score ≥ 20 (target ≥ 80%). Paired comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation (r) as effect size. RESULTS: One hundred patients were evaluated, yielding 200 report evaluations. Of 100 structured report evaluations, 98.0% (95% Clopper-Pearson CI: 93.0-99.8%) achieved an overall score ≥ 20, exceeding the 80% threshold, vs 78.0% (95% CI: 68.6-85.7%) for narrative reports. Structured reports scored significantly higher on all five general items and on the overall score (all p < 0.05), with the largest effects for readability (r = 0.95) and brevity (r = 0.85). The advantage was consistent across reader type, disease stage, and centre, with the strongest effect in locally advanced disease. Q6 (cervical stromal invasion) had the lowest feature-specific satisfaction (73.7% scoring ≥ 4), prompting template revision. CONCLUSION: A structured MRI report for cervical cancer staging significantly outperformed narrative reporting across all quality domains in a multicentre crossover design. KEY POINTS: Question Cervical cancer management is highly stage-dependent, yet evidence on clinician-centred benefit of structured vs narrative MRI staging reports in routine practice is scarce. Findings In a multicentre crossover study, a FIGO-anchored structured MRI report significantly outperformed narrative reporting on all five general quality domains. Clinical relevance A structured MRI report standardises the communication of staging features that drive cervical cancer management and is preferred by referring clinicians over narrative reporting across specialties, disease stages, and European centres.
authors: Structured Report in Cervical Cancer (StReCC) study group

articles.title: Targeting PDGFRβ from radiopharmacy to nuclear medicine: Translational implementation of [68Ga]Ga-ATH001 PET/CT at an academic center.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Positron emission tomography (PET) enables non-invasive whole-body assessment of molecular biomarkers and is particularly valuable for evaluating heterogeneous diseases such as cancer. Platelet-derived growth factor receptor beta (PDGFRβ) is a stromal biomarker expressed on activated pericytes and fibroblasts that contributes to tumour remodelling, vascular regulation and therapeutic resistance. This study describes the translational implementation of the PDGFRβ-targeting PET tracer [68Ga]Ga-ATH001, from GMP-compliant radiopharmaceutical development to its first reported oncology application in patients with liver tumours. METHODS: A GMP-compliant automated synthesis of [68Ga]Ga-ATH001 was established using a ModularLab PharmTracer synthesizer and validated for clinical use. The tracer was prospectively implemented in the IMAGINE-1 study (EU CT 2025-522290-11-00). PET imaging included dynamic liver acquisition immediately after injection, followed by whole-body PET/CT imaging and delayed liver scans to assess tracer biodistribution, tumour uptake and tracer kinetics. RESULTS: [68Ga]Ga-ATH001 was successfully translated into clinical production using an automated in-house synthesis process, achieving a decay-corrected radiochemical yield of 51.9 ± 0.7 %, radiochemical purity of 97 %, radiochemical stability of 96.3 ± 0.5 % after 2 h at room temperature and apparent molar activity of 47.2 ± 1.6 GBq/µmol at EOS. Three consecutive production runs assessed reproducibility; a fourth batch served as a microbiological worst-case challenge and was excluded from the assessment. PET/CT imaging in three patients with colorectal liver metastases showed SUVpeak tumour-to-background ratios of 1.5 to 1.8 at 60 min after injection. CONCLUSION: GMP-compliant production enabled the first reported oncology application of [68Ga]Ga-ATH001 in patients with liver tumours. The ongoing phase 1 IMAGINE-1 study will further evaluate its clinical potential. EU TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Information system: CTIS, EU CT 2025-522290-11-00, Registered 29 September 2025, IMAGINE-1 | 2025-522290-11-00 | CTIS.eu.

articles.title: What makes endolymphatic hydrops MRI work: a visual guide to better protocol choices.
articles.abstract: Endolymphatic hydrops MRI is used for the diagnostic evaluation of patients with primary or secondary endolymphatic hydrops. Delayed intravenous post-Gd 3-dimensional fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (3D-FLAIR) and 3-dimensional real inversion recovery (3D-real IR) sequences are the most widely applied techniques, because they exploit subtle Gd-related signal differences between perilymph and endolymph. Yet image quality and diagnostic confidence depend on protocol design, and variation persists between institutions, scanners, and vendors. This educational review provides a visually oriented, practical framework for optimising endolymphatic hydrops MRI, focusing on three core determinants: acquisition parameters, post-processing strategies, and contrast-agent selection. The physical principles underlying key sequence-parameter choices are explained, including the use of long echo trains to maximise acquisition efficiency, prolonged repetition times to enhance the perilymphatic signal, and inversion times tailored to the selected repetition time to achieve effective suppression of the endolymphatic signal. Representative graphs and imaging examples illustrate how protocol modifications influence contrast and diagnostic performance. The review further discusses post-processing approaches and emerging artificial intelligence-based techniques, including deep learning reconstruction, as tools to improve image quality, shorten scan time, or support higher spatial resolution. Finally, the role of gadolinium-based contrast agents, scan delay, and clinical protocol design is also addressed. Four-hour delayed intravenous imaging remains the current standard, although sequence-specific timing, single- or two-step protocols, and half-dose high-relaxivity agents may offer opportunities for tailored imaging, reduced Gd exposure, and improved sustainability. By linking sequence principles to practical protocol choices, this review aims to support reproducible, high-quality hydrops MRI across clinical settings. KEY POINTS: Question Optimisation and standardisation of 3D-FLAIR and 3D-real IR protocols are essential for accurate, reproducible assessment of endolymphatic hydrops across institutions, scanner platforms, and vendors. Findings Use TE 500-700 ms and a long echo train for efficiency/background suppression, TR ~ 16,000 ms to enhance perilymph, and TI 2400-3000 ms to suppress endolymph. Critical relevance statement Emerging deep-learning reconstruction techniques may shorten acquisition times or improve spatial resolution, while half-dose, high-relaxivity GBCAs may provide hydrops visualisation comparable to higher-dose conventional contrast protocols.

articles.title: Automated Severity Grading of Lumbar Spinal Stenosis on Sagittal MRI Using a Two-Stage Deep Learning Framework with External Clinical Validation.
articles.abstract: Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) is a prevalent degenerative condition and a major cause of disability in aging populations. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the preferred modality for assessment; however, severity grading remains inconsistent across readers and institutions, limiting reproducibility and complicating clinical decision-making. This study presents LSS-Net, a two-stage deep learning framework for automated grading of central canal stenosis using sagittal T2-weighted MRI. The first stage performs vertebral localization using a single-stage object detector, enabling standardized extraction of intervertebral regions of interest. The second stage applies a Swin Transformer-based classifier to predict stenosis severity (Normal/Mild, Moderate, Severe). The framework was developed using a multi-center dataset of 1,975 studies and evaluated on a held-out subset. Vertebral localization achieved 97.9% F1-score, while severity classification reached a weighted F1-score of 77.1%. Performance was highest for Normal/Mild and Severe classes, with reduced accuracy observed in Moderate cases, reflecting known diagnostic ambiguity. External clinical validation was conducted on an independent dataset using two expert readers. The model demonstrated substantial agreement with a neurosurgeon (accuracy 75.1%, κ = 0.73  ) and moderate agreement with a neuroradiologist (accuracy 51.0%, κ = 0.56  ), with inter-expert agreement in a comparable range. These findings suggest that LSS-Net may support more consistent and reproducible LSS grading. However, performance limitations in borderline cases and the restricted use of single-slice sagittal input highlight the need for further validation and extension to multi-sequence and multi-compartment analysis before clinical deployment.

articles.title: Association of Advanced Age With Functional Recovery After Endovascular Thrombectomy in Patients With Large-core Ischemic Stroke.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Evidence supporting endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for large-core ischemic stroke has expanded, but outcomes in patients aged ≥80 years remain insufficiently characterized. We evaluated outcomes after EVT in this population, with particular attention to prestroke disability-adjusted functional recovery. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with anterior-circulation large vessel occlusion and large-core stroke (Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score 0 to 5 or CT perfusion core volume ≥50 mL) treated with EVT between October 2019 and September 2025. The primary outcome was prestroke disability-adjusted functional recovery, defined as 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) ≤ prestroke mRS + 1. RESULTS: Among 377 patients, 75 were aged ≥80 years, and 302 were <80 years. Functional recovery occurred in 14.7% and 18.9%, respectively. Age ≥80 years was not significantly associated with functional recovery (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.00; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.45-2.22; p = 0.992). Patients aged ≥80 years had lower odds of mRS 0 to 3 (aOR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.21-0.79) and higher odds of mortality (aOR, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.01-3.16). Successful reperfusion and hemorrhagic outcomes did not differ significantly between groups. Each 10-year increase in age was associated with lower odds of functional recovery (aOR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.46-0.77). CONCLUSION: Among selected patients aged ≥80 years with large-core ischemic stroke, successful reperfusion and functional recovery remained achievable after EVT, despite poorer conventional functional outcomes and higher mortality. Advancing age was associated with progressively worse outcomes when modeled continuously. These findings support individualized prognostic assessment after EVT rather than reliance on chronological age alone.

articles.title: Uterine Artery Embolization for Fibroids with and Without Coexistent Adenomyosis: A Large U.S. Commercial Claims Comparative Effectiveness Study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare short-term safety and long-term durability of uterine artery embolization (UAE) in patients with fibroid-only disease versus those with fibroids and coexistent adenomyosis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective comparative effectiveness study of 13,098 patients aged 30-55 years undergoing UAE, identified from the MarketScan Commercial Database (2013-2025) and stratified by fibroid-only disease versus coexistent adenomyosis identified from administrative diagnosis codes. 30-day major adverse events (MAE) were compared using inverse probability of treatment weighted (IPTW) logistic regression. Long-term durability was evaluated through time-to-event analyses for any reintervention and for hysterectomy using IPTW-weighted Cox regression. RESULTS: No statistically significant difference in 30-day MAE was observed between cohorts (adjusted odds ratio 1.20; 95% CI 0.88-1.64; p = 0.24). Patients with coexistent fibroids and adenomyosis faced a higher hazard of hysterectomy (HR = 1.41; 95% CI 1.15-1.74, p = 0.001) and a borderline higher hazard of any reintervention (HR = 1.21; 95% CI 1.00-1.47, p = 0.046) compared with fibroids alone; only the hysterectomy association remained significant in all sensitivity analyses. At five years, the cumulative incidence of hysterectomy was 20.5% versus 13.9%, an absolute difference of 6.6 percentage points. CONCLUSION: No statistically significant difference in 30-day major adverse events was observed between groups. Coexistent adenomyosis was associated with a higher long-term hazard of hysterectomy, with a borderline association for any reintervention; estimates beyond five years are limited by short median follow-up and fewer patients remaining at risk.

articles.title: Upper airway morphometry in acute neck infections: Clinical associations and deep learning-based segmentation.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Upper airway (UA) compromise is a significant and potentially life-threatening complication of acute neck infection (ANI), but objective, quantitative imaging features are lacking. This study aimed to evaluate the association between UA morphometry in emergency neck MRI and disease severity in ANI, and to develop and evaluate a deep learning (DL)-based model for automatic UA segmentation in ANI patients. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A total of 322 patients were included. UA lumen was manually segmented, and prespecified morphometric features were extracted. UA morphometry was correlated with clinical outcomes. Interobserver agreement for all extracted features was evaluated with the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). An nnU-Net model was trained on manually segmented data, and its performance was evaluated using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and feature-specific ICCs. RESULTS: ICU admission occurred in 33/322 patients (10.2 %) and prolonged stay (>5 days) in 47/319 (14.7 %). Minimum cross-sectional area, compactness, maximum midline shift, and length of airway narrowing were associated with ICU admission (false-discovery-rate q ≤ 0.008) but not with prolonged stay, and did not significantly improve an established clinical model (AUC 0.80 to 0.84, DeLong p = 0.07 to 0.12). Interobserver agreement was moderate-to-excellent. The nnU-Net reached a median DSC of 0.920 with ICCs of 0.853 to 0.973 and reproduced the ICU associations. CONCLUSION: Quantitative UA morphometry in ANI is reproducible. A narrow caliber, a long narrowed segment, and lateral displacement of the airway are associated with ICU admission, without demonstrated incremental value over established predictors in the prespecified comparison. nnU-Net segmentation reproduces the features and their univariable associations.

articles.title: High-resolution proton-density MRI versus time-of-flight MRA for visualizing small circle-of-Willis arteries: Comparison with three-dimensional rotational angiography.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: High-resolution proton-density imaging (HR-PD) is a noninvasive technique for visualizing small intracranial arteries. We compared visualization of small arteries of the circle-of-Willis between HR-PD and high-resolution time-of-flight MR angiography source images (Source-MRA), with three-dimensional rotational angiography source images (Source-3D RA) as a comparator. METHODS: This retrospective study included 183 patients (mean age, 55.6 ± 11.6 years; 140 women) evaluated between November 2022 and July 2024. On a 3-point scale, two readers scored the superior hypophyseal (SHA), ophthalmic (OA), posterior communicating (Pcom), anterior choroidal (AChA), and anterior communicating (Acom) arteries on HR-PD and Source-MRA, and a third reader scored Source-3D RA. Artery-specific HR-PD versus Source-MRA differences were estimated with patient-clustered generalized estimating equations. P values were Holm-adjusted. Comparisons with Source-3D RA and interreader agreement (Gwet's AC2) were summarized. RESULTS: HR-PD scored higher than Source-MRA for the SHA (net proportion of sets scored higher on HR-PD, 0.48; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.43, 0.54), Pcom, AChA, and Acom (0.31, 0.07, and 0.11, respectively) and lower for the OA (-0.69; 95% CI: -0.74, -0.64; Holm-adjusted P < 0.001 for all five arteries). Relative to Source-3D RA, the net proportion was 0.25 (SHA), 0.22 (Pcom), -0.02 (AChA), 0.06 (Acom), and - 0.80 (OA). AC2 for HR-PD was 0.58 (SHA), 0.34 (OA), and 0.93-0.97 otherwise. CONCLUSION: HR-PD depicted the SHA, Pcom, AChA, and Acom better than Source-MRA, with the largest differences at the SHA and Pcom. The OA was depicted less well on HR-PD than on Source-MRA.

articles.title: Pediatric Bow Hunter syndrome: clinical, vascular, and longitudinal findings from a single center and systematic review of the literature.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Bow Hunter syndrome (BHS) is a rare cause of pediatric vertebral artery dissection (VAD) and posterior circulation arterial ischemic stroke (AIS) due to dynamic compression during head rotation. Imaging features, vascular evolution, and outcomes remain poorly defined. METHODS: We reviewed children with definite or probable BHS diagnosed at a tertiary pediatric center between 2010 and 2026. A systematic review identified published pediatric cases (0-18 years) of definite/probable BHS. RESULTS: Twelve boys were included (mean age, 7.3 years; mean follow-up, 54.4 months). Posterior circulation AIS occurred in 10/12 (83.3%), with multifocal infarcts of different ages in eight and additional anterior circulation embolic infarcts in three. VAD was bilateral in 6/12 (50%), consistently involving V3. Distal posterior cerebral and/or superior cerebellar artery stenosis or occlusion with collateral networks occurred in 7/12 (58.3%); basilar artery involvement in 4/12. Dynamic vascular imaging demonstrated position-dependent vertebral artery compromise in 9/12 patients (eight by rotational DSA and one by Doppler ultrasound). Craniocervical junction variants were present in 10/12 (83.3%), without flexion-extension instability. Early recurrent AIS occurred in 5/10 despite antithrombotic therapy. Serial imaging showed early vascular evolution followed by stabilization. Two patients underwent surgery; the others were treated conservatively. CONCLUSIONS: A rotational mechanical mechanism should be considered in children with posterior circulation AIS and V3 abnormalities, particularly when preceded by overlooked prodromal symptoms or minor trauma- and sport-related triggers. Multimodal neurovascular imaging, especially dynamic angiography, is essential for diagnosis, surveillance, and individualized treatment planning aimed at preventing further vascular injury.

articles.title: Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome: expanding the neuroimaging spectrum in a tertiary single-center cohort.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To characterize the neuroimaging spectrum of nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (NBCCS), with particular emphasis on cerebellar abnormalities. METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated cranial computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging examinations of patients with clinically and/or genetically confirmed NBCCS followed at a tertiary center between 2008 and 2023. Studies were independently reviewed by an experienced neuroradiologist and a radiology resident. Dural calcifications, odontogenic keratocysts, intracranial tumors, cerebellar morphology, and other structural abnormalities were assessed together with clinical and genetic findings. RESULTS: Seventeen patients (10 males and 7 females; age range, 1-70 years) were included. Dural calcification was detected in 13 of 16 evaluable patients (81.3%), while maxillary and/or mandibular odontogenic keratocysts were present in 10 of 13 patients with dedicated maxillofacial computed tomography (76.9%). Macrocerebellum was identified in 5 of 13 evaluable patients (38,4%), cerebellar dysplasia in 3 of 13 (23.1%) and olfactory bulb hypoplasia was observed in 7 of 13 (53.8%). Cerebellar tonsillar ectopia and ventriculomegaly were each observed in 7 of 17 patients (41.2%), and persistent cavum septi pellucidi in 3 of 17 (17.6%). Intracranial neoplasms included two meningiomas and one previously treated medulloblastoma. CONCLUSION: Cerebellar abnormalities, particularly macrocerebellum and cerebellar dysplasia, may be underrecognized components of the neuroimaging phenotype of NBCCS. Awareness of these findings may support syndromic recognition and appropriate clinical and genetic evaluation.

articles.title: A machine learning approach to MRI screening for brain arteriovenous malformations in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is an inherited vascular disorder characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in multiple organs. Although brain MRI screening is recommended in all patients with HHT, in many centers, this may be difficult to implement due to organizational constraints. The aim of this study was to develop a machine learning model to predict the presence of bAVMs and other cerebrovascular malformations in patients with HHT, with the goal of supporting risk stratification in centers where genotype information is already available and identifying patients who may benefit from closer and more conservative surveillance. METHODS: All patients with confirmed diagnosis of HHT, complete genetic work-up, and radiological screening (2018-2026) were included for the analysis. Two end points were defined: probability of detecting bAVMs, and probability of detecting any cerebrovascular findings. Analysis was performed using Python and R. RESULTS: A total of 142 patients with confirmed HHT (meeting ≥ 3 Curaçao criteria) were included. For bAVM prediction, both models showed good discrimination, with an AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.73-0.94) for Logistic Regression (LR) and 0.85 (95% CI: 0.74-0.96) for Random Forest (RF). Despite the slightly higher AUC, RF showed lower specificity, PPV, and F1 score, higher sensitivity (0.73 vs. 0.69) and same NPV. LR also showed better calibration, with an intercept of -0.30 (95% CI: -1.38-0.78) and slope of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.34-1.40), compared with 1.39 (95% CI: -0.46-3.23) and 2.39 (95% CI: 0.64-4.15), respectively, for RF. In contrast, models predicting overall cerebrovascular malformations showed limited discrimination and poor calibration with both LR and RF. For bAVM prediction, LR identified deletion mutations, ENG, family history, ACVRL1, and truncated variants as the most influential features, while RF SHAP analysis highlighted ACVRL1, ENG, age, pulmonary AVMs, and family history. CONCLUSION: Effective risk stratification was achieved by the phenotype-specific bAVM model, supporting its potential applicability. Upon external validation this tool may enable an efficient allocation of screening strategies.

articles.title: Ultrasound-derived fat fraction and shear wave elastography for liver assessment in bariatric surgery candidates: diagnostic performance and longitudinal changes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of ultrasound-derived fat fraction (UDFF) and auto-point shear wave elastography (Auto-pSWE) in bariatric surgery candidates, identify biological variables independently associated with their values and monitor postoperative changes in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) patients. METHODS: This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent UDFF and Auto-pSWE examinations within 3 days before bariatric surgery (October 2023-February 2025), with intraoperative biopsy as reference. Diagnostic performance of UDFF and Auto-pSWE (which measured shear wave velocity, SWV) were analyzed by receiver operating characteristic analysis. Multivariable generalized linear models identified variables independently associated with UDFF and SWV. Postoperative follow-ups were conducted at 3 and 6 months in MASLD patients. RESULTS: A total of 237 patients (mean age, 29.42 ± 9.37; 98 men) were included. UDFF showed excellent diagnostic performance for steatosis grades (AUCs: 0.991 for ≥S1, 0.911 for ≥S2, and 0.831 for ≥S3), with steatosis percentage as the strongest independent correlate (partial R2=0.302). SWV exhibited moderate diagnostic performance for significant fibrosis (AUC = 0.752), with fibrosis stages and alanine aminotransferase showing similar independent explanatory power (partial R2=0.067 and 0.063, respectively). In 104 MASLD patients, median UDFF decreased substantially by approximately 80% at 6 months while SWV transiently rose at 3 months before returning to a level comparable to baseline at 6 months. CONCLUSION: UDFF provides accurate assessment of steatosis and shows potential for postoperative monitoring, whereas Auto-pSWE demonstrates moderate performance for significant fibrosis and transient postoperative changes, supporting its complementary rather than standalone role.

articles.title: Enhanced image quality and interpretation efficiency of voxelwise-computed diffusion-weighted imaging for bladder cancer VI-RADS assessment.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is central to bladder cancer assessment with the Vesical Imaging-Reporting and Data System (VI-RADS). Computed diffusion-weighted imaging (cDWI) reduces scan time but has limited signal-to-noise ratio (SNR); its voxelwise variant, voxelwise-computed diffusion-weighted imaging (vcDWI), may overcome this limitation. We evaluated whether vcDWI provides better image quality and shorter interpretation time while maintaining diagnostic accuracy compared with acquired DWI (aDWI) in VI-RADS assessment. METHODS: This single-center study included 111 consecutive patients with bladder cancer who underwent magnetic resonance imaging between October 2019 and October 2024. Two radiologists (2 and 5 years' experience) assessed image quality and objective metrics: tumor SNR (SNRtumor), urine-referenced SNR, contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and urine-referenced contrast ratio (CR, the ratio of tumor to urine signal intensity); they performed VI-RADS scoring and recorded interpretation times. Diagnostic performance for muscle invasion (VI-RADS ≥ 4) was evaluated against histopathology. RESULTS: vcDWI showed higher urine-referenced SNR and contrast ratio than all aDWI sequences (all p < 0.001), with CNR comparable to b = 1400 s/mm², whereas lesion-only SNRtumor was lower than at b = 700 and b = 1400 s/mm². It received superior subjective scores for lesion clarity and overall image quality (all p < 0.001). Diagnostic performance was comparable, with the difference in area under the curve (AUC) within a 0.10 non-inferiority margin in an exploratory post hoc analysis (AUCs, vcDWI vs. aDWI: 0.86 vs. 0.85 and 0.90 vs. 0.91; one-sided 95% upper bounds 0.030 and 0.054). vcDWI reduced interpretation time (median times 16.0% and 28.6% lower; p < 0.001), and inter-observer agreement was good for aDWI and excellent for vcDWI (weighted κ = 0.797 vs. 0.895). CONCLUSIONS: vcDWI improved tumor conspicuity and background suppression, was compatible with non-inferiority to aDWI in an exploratory analysis, and reduced interpretation time in VI-RADS assessment, with good-to-excellent inter-observer agreement.

articles.title: Exploring performance and trust in autonomous surgical robotic systems: the role of visuo-haptic guidance.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Incorporating task-level autonomy into teleoperation systems for robot assisted laparoscopic surgery requires operators to effectively manage transitions from task-level autonomy to teleoperation control, particularly during system failures. This study investigated the impact of the level of guidance during take-over situations on participants' performance and their trust in the teleoperation system. METHODS: N = 34 students, unfamiliar with the system and task, performed a ring transfer task under two conditions: visual guidance, where they monitored the system visually, and visuo-haptic guidance, where they also received haptic feedback by holding the input device as the system operated in task-level autonomy. During some trials, system failures occurred, requiring participants to take over control. RESULTS: Results showed that participants noticed system failures faster with visuo-haptic guidance compared to visual guidance. Although visuo-haptic guidance did not improve task completion times or accuracy during task completion, it led to significantly higher trust in the teleoperation system and a stronger sense of perceived control. However, participants also reported higher physical demand and effort under visuo-haptic guidance, indicating an increased workload in this condition. CONCLUSION: In conclusion, these findings reveal important trade-offs of the influence of haptic guidance during human oversight of teleoperated autonomous systems.

articles.title: Diffusion MRI-Based Fetal Thermometry Using Cerebrospinal Fluid: A Translational Feasibility Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Noninvasive fetal temperature assessment could improve MRI safety monitoring and provide insight into fetal physiology. Diffusion MRI is a potential approach because water diffusivity in free fluids is temperature dependent. However, the applicability of adult-derived diffusivity-temperature calibration to neonatal and fetal CSF remains uncertain. PURPOSE: To evaluate the feasibility of diffusion MRI for noninvasive estimation of a diffusion-derived proxy of fetal temperature in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). STUDY TYPE: Prospective feasibility study. POPULATION/SUBJECTS: 11 preterm neonates (postmenstrual age, 30.0-40.6 weeks; 5 male, 6 female) underwent CSF diffusion MRI for translational validation, and 11 fetuses (gestational age, 27.6-37.6 weeks) underwent CSF diffusion MRI for in utero feasibility assessment. FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 1.5T monopolar spin-echo echo-planar diffusion imaging for neonatal validation; 3T monopolar spin-echo echo-planar diffusion MRI for fetal imaging. ASSESSMENT: Temperature was derived from CSF apparent diffusion coefficients using an established diffusivity-temperature calibration. Neonatal estimates were compared with pre and postscan axillary temperatures. Monte Carlo simulations evaluated the effects of noise, gradient-amplitude scaling errors, and calibration uncertainty. STATISTICAL TESTS: Bland-Altman analysis, linear regression, descriptive statistics, Huber M-estimation, and Monte Carlo simulations were performed. Statistical significance for regression analyses was defined as p < 0.05. RESULTS: Diffusion-derived CSF temperatures agreed with axillary measurements within approximately ±1°C in 11 preterm neonates and showed Bland-Altman biases of 0.41°C and 0.50°C for mean diffusion-derived temperature compared with pre and postscan axillary measurements, respectively. In 11 fetuses, the CSF temperature estimates using the Huber M-estimator were 37.13°C ± 0.41°C (mean ± SD). Monte Carlo simulations revealed a decrease in the temperature SD from about 4.5°C at SNR = 30 to 1.6°C at SNR = 80. Gradient-amplitude scaling errors of ±8% resulted in approximately 6.5°C-7°C absolute temperature bias, which was reduced to ≤ 0.1°C after ideal effective b value correction. DATA CONCLUSION: Diffusion MRI enables feasible estimation of a diffusion-derived proxy of fetal temperature in CSF. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 1.

articles.title: Selective Size Imaging via Diffusion MRI for Preoperative IDH Mutation Status, Grading, and Progression-Free Survival Risk Stratification in Adult-Type Diffuse Glioma.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Selective size imaging using filters through diffusion times (SSIFT) MRI provides cell size-weighted contrast, but its value in adult-type diffuse gliomas remains unclear. PURPOSE: To evaluate SSIFT MRI for preoperative isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status assessment, World Health Organization (WHO) central nervous system (CNS) grading and progression-free survival (PFS) risk stratification were compared with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) metrics. STUDY TYPE: Prospective, single-center. POPULATION: Seventy-one patients with pathologically confirmed adult-type diffuse gliomas (median age, 52 years; 42 men, 29 women) with Grades 2, 3, and 4 gliomas (n = 17, 12, and 42). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3 T; conventional MRI included T1-weighted imaging, T2-weighted FLAIR imaging, and diffusion-weighted imaging with ADC mapping. Oscillating and pulsed gradient spin-echo diffusion encoding. ASSESSMENT: Whole-solid-tumor regions of interest were delineated, and extracted metrics were compared to pathologic and molecular findings. SSIFT-derived incremental area under the curve (iAUC) quantified normalized diffusion-weighted signal changes with diffusion time. Extracted metrics included mean and 90th-percentile iAUC values (iAUC_mean, iAUC_90Percentile) and mean and 10th-percentile ADC values (ADC_mean, ADC_10Percentile). STATISTICAL TESTS: Kruskal-Wallis and Jonckheere-Terpstra tests, ROC analysis with paired DeLong tests, Cox regression, Kaplan-Meier analysis, and bootstrap comparison of integrated time-dependent AUC (AUCint). p < 0.05 indicated statistical significance. RESULTS: Both iAUC metrics yielded AUCs of 0.839 for IDH assessment (95% confidence intervals [CIs], 0.731-0.938 and 0.731-0.941), significantly outperforming ADC_mean (0.697; 0.573-0.821). iAUC_90Percentile differentiated Grade 2 from Grade 3 gliomas (AUC = 0.789; 95% CI: 0.571-0.966) and outperformed ADC_10Percentile (AUC = 0.520; 95% CI: 0.284-0.722). During median follow-up of 469 days, 26 patients progressed. iAUC_mean remained significantly associated with PFS after multivariable adjustment (HR = 1.206; 95% CI: 1.048-1.387). Adding iAUC_mean increased bootstrapped AUCint from 0.788 to 0.815, although the increase was not significant (ΔAUCint = 0.027; 95% CI: -0.003 to 0.078; p = 0.0899). DATA CONCLUSION: SSIFT-derived iAUC might provide cell size-related microstructural information complementary to ADC and may aid preoperative IDH mutation status assessment and glioma grading. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 1. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 2.

articles.title: Separation of Diamagnetic and Paramagnetic Susceptibility Sources in Liver Using DECOMPOSE-QSM.
articles.abstract: Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) enables noninvasive assessment of liver iron based on its paramagnetic properties. However, the paramagnetic contribution of iron can be confounded by the competing diamagnetic sources within the same voxel, particularly collagen in fibrotic tissue. Magnetic source separation techniques can disentangle these opposing susceptibility effects within a voxel, potentially enabling independent detection of iron and collagen. In this study, we conducted an initial evaluation of DECOMPOSE-QSM using abdominal multi-echo MRI data from a small patient cohort with normal to moderate liver iron overload (N = 19) and varying degrees of fibrosis (N = 3). Source-separated paramagnetic susceptibility showed a stronger correlation with liver iron concentration (R2 = 0.86, p < 0.05), whereas conventional QSM exhibited a weaker correlation (R2 = 0.28, p = 0.08) in patients with normal to moderate iron overload. Furthermore, preliminary results in a small fibrotic cohort demonstrated that source-separated diamagnetic susceptibility exhibit trends comparable to conventional QSM, suggesting that the method preserves sensitivity to fibrosis-related tissue components.

articles.title: Habitat Imaging with Virtual MR Elastography and CTRW Diffusion Model for Predicting Postoperative Pancreatic Fistula in Pancreatic Cancer.
articles.abstract: The preoperative prediction of clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF) is crucial for the implementation of efficient prevention strategies in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Our study aimed to explore the value of habitat imaging employing virtual magnetic resonance elastography (vMRE) and continuous-time random-walk (CTRW) diffusion MRI for preoperatively predicting CR-POPF in PDAC after pancreaticoduodenectomy. vMRE reflected pancreatic stiffness, whereas CTRW-derived parameters characterized non-Gaussian water diffusion and microstructural heterogeneity. Their voxel-wise integration could identify imaging-defined phenotype reflecting complementary tissue properties. Patients with suspected PDAC who underwent pancreatic MRI were prospectively collected. Multiple-b-value diffusion-weighted imaging sequence was acquired and fitted to CTRW model. The diffusion-based tissue shear modulus (μdiff) was calculated by calibrating the shifted apparent diffusion coefficient (sADC) with standard MR elastography (MRE). The presumed pancreatic stump was segmented into various subregions by habitat analysis employing two combinations of vMRE and CTRW parameter maps. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify the independent factors and construct the prediction models. The predictive performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve and validated using bootstrap method. A total of 183 patients were finally included, and 36 patients (19.67%) developed CR-POPF. The optimism-corrected area under the curve (AUC) of two combined models was 0.947 (95% CI, 0.898-0.987) and 0.897 (95% CI, 0.832-0.962) respectively, through bootstrap validation. Habitat analysis using vMRE and CTRW diffusion model provided complementary characterization of stiffness and diffusion heterogeneity, and exhibited great potential for the preoperative prediction of CR-POPF in PDAC after pancreaticoduodenectomy.

articles.title: TRACER: A Multimodal Multi-agent Workflow for Transparent Chest X-ray Assistance.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation can detect abnormalities, generate reports, provide visual grounding, and support dialogue but often offer limited mechanisms for inspection and follow-up. We present Transparent Radiology Assistance for Chest X-ray Explanation and Review (TRACER), a multimodal multi-agent workflow integrating CXR analysis, consultation support, and prior-report comparison with structured findings, gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) cues, report-generation steps, and execution trajectories. Evaluation included report-quality benchmarking on 2000 frontal CXRs and user studies with 60 non-radiologist participants. Experiment II used 12 cases, with one fixed report per case in both text-only and transparency-supported conditions; the latter additionally displayed structured findings, finding-specific Grad-CAM cues, and execution trajectories. Open-ended responses were scored by an independent automated judge with clinician validation on a stratified subset. Experiment III evaluated eight prior-current pairs with or without an archive-assisted comparison paragraph. The full report pipeline achieved the best values on six of eight automatic metrics. Transparency support increased Consultation Preparation Quality from 2.133 ± 1.302 to 3.142 ± 1.154 (odds ratio 6.76, 95% confidence interval 3.92-11.67; P < 0.001  ). Archive assistance improved difference identification from 0.642±0.338 to 0.833±0.285 (odds ratio 4.16, 95% confidence interval 2.33-7.42; P < 0.001  ) and reduced mean completion time from 108.825 to 74.225 s. The transparency-supported condition also yielded higher usability ratings and lower perceived workload. These findings support TRACER as an inspectable workflow for CXR report review, verification-oriented consultation preparation, and prior-current comparison; clinical usefulness requires evaluation with patients and clinicians.

articles.title: CrossBoneNet: An Ultralightweight Hybrid CNN-ViT Architecture via Asymmetric Reversed Cross-Attention for Radiographic Fracture Detection.
articles.abstract: Misdiagnoses in emergency departments are often associated with the difficulty in interpreting radiological findings on bone fractures due to millimetric fractures, overlapping bones, or superimpositions. Despite the high efficiency of state-of-the-art models in diagnosing such cases, their massive computational requirements severely hinder their implementation on resource-constrained devices in real-world clinical settings. In this study, we propose an ultralightweight CNN-ViT model, CrossBoneNet, which is designed for edge AI compatibility with minimal memory requirements. CrossBoneNet combines local microfracture detection using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and global anatomical recognition using vision transformers (ViTs). The model merges features from both architectures using the proposed asymmetric reversed cross-attention, where CNN features act as queries and ViT features act as keys and values-to efficiently map fine-grained local anomalies into a broader global anatomical context. Operating with a minimal parameter count (0.593 M) and low computational cost (1.527 GFLOPs), CrossBoneNet achieved a PR-AUC of 0.8498 ± 0.0086 and a ROC-AUC of 0.8427 ± 0.0072 on the MURA dataset in a patient-wise isolated evaluation. It achieves highly competitive performance-remaining within a 4% margin of the 88.59 million parameter ConvNeXt-Base model-while delivering over 99% memory savings. After fine-tuning on the FracAtlas dataset, CrossBoneNet achieved a specificity of 0.9760 ± 0.0080 and PR-AUC of 0.7568 ± 0.0414, demonstrating effective cross-domain transfer learning. With a compact footprint (< 3 MB) and high specificity at the default 0.50 operating threshold, CrossBoneNet demonstrates potential as a point-of-care decision support and worklist prioritization tool on resource-constrained devices, while calibrating the decision threshold (e.g., τ = 0.3837  and τ = 0.3449  ) enables high-sensitivity screening modes (achieving 85.03% and 89.96% sensitivity on MURA, respectively), pending prospective validation. This retrospective study establishes proof of concept; future work will focus on prospective clinical trials and expansion to multiclass fracture classification.

articles.title: From Predicted Dose to Computationally Verified Plan: An End-to-End Deep Learning and Monte Carlo Pipeline for Automated VMAT Glioblastoma Radiotherapy.
articles.abstract: Deep learning dose prediction can accurately reproduce clinical dose distributions but typically stops short of generating machine-parameterized treatment plans. The present study introduces an end-to-end pipeline that converts a predicted dose into a machine-parameterized volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) approximation, evaluating dosimetric consistency via an independent Monte Carlo (MC) dose recomputation for cranial glioblastoma (GBM). A three-dimensional U-Net predicts voxel-level dose from the planning CT and structure masks. The framework was evaluated on 30 held-out test patients. Each prediction is converted into a discretized VMAT sequence via direct aperture optimization (DAO) and voxel-wise dose mimicking. This optimization is driven by a size-normalized squared-deviation objective that equalizes per-voxel optimization pressure across targets and organs at risk (OARs) of drastically different sizes. The resulting plans undergo an independent computational dose recomputation step using the ompMC photon Monte Carlo engine, reporting gamma analysis at 3%/2 mm evaluated over the high-dose (≥ 50%) and whole-field (≥ 10%) regions in accordance with TG-218 recommendations. The predicted dose matched the clinical dose to within 0.9-1.9% on PTV dose-volume metrics. The dose-mimicking pipeline successfully inverse-engineered these predictions into discretized VMAT plans that reproduced clinical PTV coverage while adhering to strict OAR tolerances. Independent Monte Carlo recomputation confirmed the dosimetric consistency of the generated plans. Utilizing a highly converged MC simulation (σ ≈ 0.8%), the high-dose-region gamma pass rate (3%/2 mm) reached a median of 98.2% [IQR 97.1-99.0%], confirming excellent agreement between the pencil-beam optimization and MC dose transport. The proposed pipeline bridges the critical gap from a deep learning-predicted dose to a machine-parameterized, computational VMAT plan. The size-normalised mimicking objective is identified as the key enabler for stable inverse-engineering. While true clinical deliverability requires further validation on a physical linear accelerator, the independent MC dose-recomputation step provides a rigorous computational QA framework that standard dose prediction studies currently omit.

articles.title: Active Learning and Cascaded nnU-Net v2 for Multi-structure Segmentation of Thoracic CT: A Single-Center Pilot Study.
articles.abstract: Accurate segmentation of thoracic structures on chest computed tomography (CT) is important for lung cancer surgery, but manual annotation is labor intensive and particularly challenging for small structures such as pulmonary vessels and nodules. We compared four nnU-Net v2-based segmentation configurations: single-stage full-data training, active learning alone, cascaded segmentation alone, and active learning combined with cascaded segmentation in a retrospective single-center cohort. This retrospective study included chest CT scans from 85 patients. In the cascaded configurations, pulmonary lobes were segmented in the first stage to provide global anatomical context, followed by refinement of the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, and nodules within the constrained region. All four configurations were evaluated using the same fixed patient-level internal test set of 30 patients, with segmentation performance assessed using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and the 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95). The full-data baseline achieved DSCs of 0.92-0.93 for the five pulmonary lobes, with lower performance for the bronchus (0.82), pulmonary vessels (0.67), and pulmonary nodules (0.78). The combined active learning and cascaded configuration improved lobar DSCs to 0.94-0.96. Compared with the baseline, DSC increased to 0.90, 0.77, and 0.86 for the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, and pulmonary nodules, respectively (all p < 0.05), while HD95 decreased from 5.4 to 2.5 mm for pulmonary vessels and from 4.8 to 2.1 mm for pulmonary nodules. In this single-center cohort, cascaded segmentation strategies showed improved internal test performance for small thoracic structures, supporting further evaluation in larger multicenter cohorts.

articles.title: A Causally Guided Imaging-Informatics Framework for Ranking DXA-Derived Hip Imaging Phenotypes in Hip Fracture Risk Prediction.
articles.abstract: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) provides multiple hip measurements, but their value for fracture risk stratification is rarely evaluated within an imaging-informatics framework. We developed a causally guided framework to rank DXA-derived hip imaging phenotypes and assess whether ranked phenotypes improve hip fracture prediction. We analyzed 21,098 UK Biobank participants with linked health records, DXA-derived hip measures, and prespecified covariates. Sixteen phenotypes spanning bone mineral content (BMC), bone mineral density (BMD), and T-score across hip-related regions were evaluated. Confounder selection was guided by a prespecified directed acyclic graph (DAG). Backdoor-adjusted average treatment effects (ATEs) were estimated on the absolute risk-difference scale per standard deviation (SD) increase. Effect heterogeneity was evaluated for total femur BMD, and prediction was assessed using clinical variables combined with ATE-ranked phenotypes. Among 21,098 participants, 115 had hip fractures. All 16 phenotypes showed negative backdoor-adjusted ATEs per SD increase. The largest ATEs were observed for total femur BMC and BMD, each with a risk difference of - 0.0047, corresponding to 4.7 fewer hip fractures per 1000 participants per SD higher phenotype value. Conditional effects of total femur BMD were stronger among older participants and those with lower BMI. Clinical variables plus the top 11 ATE-ranked phenotypes achieved higher AUC than FRAX with femoral neck BMD (0.842 vs. 0.709), with higher sensitivity (0.748 vs. 0.443) and similar specificity (0.793 vs. 0.777). DXA-derived hip phenotypes differed in backdoor-adjusted ATEs. This framework may support interpretable phenotype selection for fracture risk stratification.

articles.title: Radiomics analysis of brain-tumor interface on multiparametric MRI for prediction of brain metastasis primary site.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Brain metastasis (BM) frequently occurs in advanced cancer patients, and accurate identification of the primary origin is essential for personalized treatment. Conventional imaging often lacks sensitivity and specificity for BM source prediction. This study aimed to develop and validate a multiparametric MRI-based radiomics model emphasizing brain-tumor interface (BTI) features to improve noninvasive BM origin identification. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The primary cohort included 429 patients (740 BMs) from two centers, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), small cell lung cancer (SCLC), breast cancer (BC), and gastrointestinal cancer (GIC), and an independent validation cohort of 33 patients (84 BMs) from a third center. All underwent pre-treatment 3.0 T MRI with T1-weighted contrast-enhanced (T1CE) and T2-weighted (T2W) sequences. Radiomic features were extracted from tumor core and BTI regions (2, 4, 6, 8 mm). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for feature selection, and radiomics signatures (RS) were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. RESULTS: The constructed RS-BTI4 based on the 4-mm BTI region generated the best overall performance, with area under the ROC curve (AUCs) in the training cohort were 0.855 (LC/NLC), 0.910 (SCLC/NSCLC), and 0.890 (BC/GIC); in validation cohort, 0.726, 0.856, and 0.809; and in external validation cohort, 0.739, 0.750, and 0.792, respectively. RS-BTI4 consistently outperformed models based on other BTI radial widths and the whole tumor region in identifying the primary origin of BM. CONCLUSION: BTI-derived radiomic features demonstrate strong potential for noninvasive identification of BM origin, with the 4-mm BTI region showing optimal predictive performance. KEY POINTS: Question Conventional MRI cannot reliably identify the primary origin of brain metastases, particularly when the primary tumor remains unknown at diagnosis. Findings The 4-mm brain-tumor interface model showed the most favorable overall performance, measured by area under the curve, across three binary classification tasks and validation cohorts. Critical relevance statement Integrating brain-tumor interface radiomics with multiparametric MRI may improve noninvasive estimation of BM origin and support more targeted diagnostic evaluation in clinical radiology.

articles.title: Diagnostic accuracy of 3D MRI rendering techniques for evaluation of hourglass-like constrictions in Parsonage-Turner syndrome.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate inter-reader agreement and diagnostic accuracy of curved multiplanar reformatting (cMPR) and maximum intensity projection (MIP) techniques for detecting hourglass-like constrictions (HGCs). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Thirty brachial plexus 3-Tesla, 3D, 1-mm isotropic MR neurography (MRN) datasets (10 patients without and 20 patients with Parsonage-Turner syndrome (PTS) affecting the suprascapular nerve (SSN)) were retrospectively analyzed by four musculoskeletal radiology fellows for the number and severity of HGCs using both post-processing views in a randomized, blinded fashion. An experienced, attending radiologist served as the reference standard. Inter-reader agreement was assessed using Gwet's AC1 and intraclass correlation (ICC). Image interpretation time was compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank test. RESULTS: Inter-reader agreement for HGC presence was substantial to almost perfect among fellows (cMPR AC1 = 0.7, MIP AC1 = 0.67) and when compared to the attending (cMPR AC1 = 0.67-0.83, MIP AC1 = 0.63-0.83). Agreement for severe HGC count was substantial to almost perfect (fellows: cMPR ICC = 0.65, MIP ICC = 0.79; vs. attending: ICC = 0.62-0.83, MIP ICC = 0.69-0.88), but poor to fair for mild HGCs (fellows: cMPR ICC = 0.23, MIP ICC = 0.26; vs. attending: ICC = 0-0.21, MIP ICC = 0-0.09). Sensitivity to HGC presence was excellent (cMPR, 85-100%; MIP, 90-100%), though specificity (cMPR, 50-100%; MIP, 40-90%) and diagnostic accuracy (cMPR, 80-90%; MIP, 76-90%) varied. The MIP method required significantly less interpretation time than cMPR (median: 33 vs. 104 s, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: High inter-reader agreement and sensitivity but variable specificity for HGC detection suggest both techniques are viable tools for MRN, with cMPR better suited for detailed HGC evaluation and MIP for initial screening.

articles.title: Imaging-based quantification of myosteatosis: a narrative review of main principles, techniques, and clinical applications.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Intramuscular fat infiltration, commonly referred to as myosteatosis, has emerged as an important biomarker of skeletal muscle quality and is increasingly associated with aging, sarcopenia, metabolic disorders, neuromuscular diseases, and reduced functional outcomes. As interest in muscle composition grows, imaging techniques capable of quantifying intramuscular fat have become essential for both clinical assessment and research applications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and ultrasound (US) each provide distinct approaches for evaluating muscle fat content, relying on different physical principles, biomarkers, and quantitative frameworks. This article provides an overview of the principal imaging modalities currently used for intramuscular fat quantification, with emphasis on their physical foundations, quantitative biomarkers, methodological developments, and clinical applicability. METHODS: We conducted a literature search on Google Scholar and PubMed using the following keywords: "myosteatosis", "muscle fat", "CT", "MRI" and "ultrasound", as well as more specific topics regarding corresponding modalities, methods, or limitations encountered: "muscle attenuation", "material decomposition", "PDFF", "Dixon", "echo intensity", "echo attenuation", "speed of sound". The included papers focus on the measurements of muscle fat content using CT, MRI, or US. KEY CONTENT AND FINDINGS: This paper reviews the three main imaging modalities to assess muscle fat content: CT, MRI, and US. It details the working physical principles, and introduces the existing methods applied to assess fat content inside the muscles. While some methods are already used in clinical practice, there remain limitations that are detailed and discussed to improve the myosteatosis assessment. CONCLUSIONS: While significant progress has been made in imaging-based quantification of intramuscular fat, no single modality currently satisfies all clinical and research requirements. A nuanced understanding of each technique's strengths and limitations is essential to guide their appropriate use, and continued methodological advancements will be key to improving their reliability.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence applications in photon-counting detector CT for coronary artery disease imaging: a narrative review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) is a first-line non-invasive imaging modality for CAD evaluation, but conventional energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT) is often limited by blooming artifacts, noise, and partial-volume effects.
